Nasal vowels (ã, õ, am, em, im, on, um, etc.)

Portuguese has true nasal vowels, meaning the vowel itself is nasalized — not followed by a separate “n” or “m” sound like in English.

In English:

“man” = vowel + clear N

“song” = vowel + NG

In Portuguese:

não → the vowel itself is nasal; there is no strong N at the end

bom → not “bom” with an M sound — just a nasalized O

What English speakers do wrong:

They pronounce a clear N or M at the end.

They keep the vowel fully oral.

What to do instead:

Let air pass through your nose while saying the vowel.

Think of lightly humming the vowel.

The N/M is often just a nasal marker, not a full consonant.

If you don’t nasalize properly, you sound immediately foreign.

Open vs closed vowels (é vs ê, ó vs ô)

Portuguese distinguishes between open and closed mid vowels, and this can change meaning.

Examples:

avó (grandmother) vs avô (grandfather)

pode (can) vs pôde (could)

English speakers often:

Collapse both into one generic “eh” or “oh.”

Don’t hear the distinction clearly.

The difference:

Open (é, ó) → lower, more relaxed, slightly wider mouth.

Closed (ê, ô) → higher tongue, more controlled, tenser sound.

This is subtle but important. It’s not dramatic — it’s precise.

R sounds (very variable)

Portuguese R is one of the biggest accent markers.

Initial R or “rr” → guttural /ʁ/

Similar to French R or German uvular R.

rio

rua

carro

Produced in the throat, not with the tongue tip.

English speakers often:

Use an English R (retroflex).

Don’t make it guttural enough.

Single R between vowels → tap /ɾ/

caro

para

barato

This is like the quick Spanish single R or the American English “t” in “butter.”

English speakers often:

Use a heavy English R.

Don’t tap quickly enough.

Final R (Brazilian Portuguese)

In many Brazilian accents:

Final R becomes a guttural /ʁ/ or weakened sound.

falar

comer

viver

English speakers often:

Drop it completely.

Or pronounce a strong American R.

D / T before i or e → palatalized

In Brazilian Portuguese:

dia → /ˈdʒiɐ/

tia → /ˈtʃiɐ/

D + i/e becomes like English “j”
T + i/e becomes like English “ch”

English speakers often:

Keep hard /d/ and /t/

Say “dee-a” instead of “jee-a”

This is extremely common in Brazil and crucial for sounding natural.
